title: Ezekiel 9:1–11
context: Ezekiel 9:1–11 is told by the prophet. The LORD cries out for those in charge of the city to draw near with their weapons, and six men come from the upper gate, with a man clothed in linen among them carrying a writer’s inkhorn (9:1–2). Linen recalls priestly garments (compare Leviticus 16:4), and a figure clothed in linen also appears in Daniel 10:5; these are named without identifying the figures. The glory of the God of Israel goes up from the cherub to the threshold of the house (9:3). The LORD tells the man in linen to set a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and cry over the abominations (9:4). The word rendered mark is commonly noted to be the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, taw, but these notes make no claim about its shape. The mark is a sign of mercy within judgment, and both traditions read it as shared ground; it may be read alongside the blood on the doors in Exodus 12:13 and the sealing of God’s servants in Revelation 7:3 and 9:4, named here without harmonizing. Questions about sealing and perseverance belong to the existing boxes at Revelation 7:3 and Ephesians 1:13 and are not reopened here. The others are told to strike without pity, sparing those with the mark, and to “Begin at my sanctuary” (9:5–6); some readers hear an echo in 1 Peter 4:17, “For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God.”, a hedged connection rather than a claim of direct reference (compare Jeremiah 25:29). This is a vision of judgment, and the notes describe it with sobriety. While the killing goes on, Ezekiel falls on his face and cries, “Ah Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the residue of Israel in your pouring out of your wrath on Jerusalem?” (9:8; compare 11:13). The LORD answers that the iniquity is exceedingly great, quoting again the saying, “The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD doesn’t see” (9:9; compare 8:12). The man in linen reports, “I have done as you have commanded me.” (9:11).

verses.text: Then he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying, “Cause those who are in charge of the city to draw near, each man with his destroying weapon in his hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD cries in Ezekiel’s ears for those in charge of the city to draw near, each with his destroying weapon. Arminian readers note that the vision turns from the exposure of sin to judgment, and they read the summons soberly as the announcement that the LORD’s patience has reached its limit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same turn and observe that the executioners act only at the LORD’s command, which places the judgment under his authority. They read the verse with sobriety as part of a vision of judgment, not as a narrative of an actual massacre in that moment.

verses.text: Behold, six men came from the way of the upper gate, which lies toward the north, every man with his slaughter weapon in his hand. One man in the middle of them was clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkhorn by his side. They went in, and stood beside the bronze altar.
verses.arminianNotes: Six men come from the upper gate with weapons, and among them is a man clothed in linen with a writer’s inkhorn, and they stand beside the bronze altar. Arminian readers note that linen recalls priestly garments (compare Leviticus 16:4), and they hold the figure’s identity open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the figure’s identity loosely and note that a man clothed in linen also appears in Daniel 10:5, named without identifying the two. They observe that the scribe’s inkhorn prepares for the marking of the faithful, which comes before the judgment.

verses.text: The glory of the God of Israel went up from the cherub, whereupon it was, to the threshold of the house; and he called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writer’s inkhorn by his side.
verses.arminianNotes: The glory of the God of Israel went up from the cherub to the threshold of the house, and the LORD called to the man clothed in linen. Arminian readers note that this is the first stage of the glory’s departure, and they see God reluctantly moving from the heart of the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same first stage, from the cherub to the threshold, which is repeated in 10:4. They read the movement as the beginning of the glory’s departure that continues to the east gate (10:18–19) and the mountain east of the city (11:22–23).

verses.text: The LORD said to him, “Go through the middle of the city, through the middle of Jerusalem, and set a mark on the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry over all the abominations that are done within it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the man in linen to set a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and cry over the abominations. Arminian readers see mercy within judgment, and they compare Exodus 12:13, “When I see the blood, I will pass over you”, named without harmonizing, as shared ground.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the mark as mercy within judgment and compare Revelation 7:3 and 9:4, named without harmonizing. They note that the word for mark is commonly noted to be the name of the letter taw, and they point to the existing boxes at Revelation 7:3 and Ephesians 1:13 rather than opening a new contrast.

verses.text: To the others he said in my hearing, “Go through the city after him, and strike. Don’t let your eye spare, neither have pity.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the others to go through the city after the man in linen and strike, without sparing or pity. Arminian readers note that the order follows the marking, so that mercy comes first, and they read the severity of judgment soberly in the setting of a vision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same order and read it as showing that God distinguishes between those who grieve over sin and those who take part in it. They observe that the command is part of a visionary scene and both traditions read it with sobriety, without dwelling on its violence.

verses.text: Kill utterly the old man, the young man, the virgin, little children and women; but don’t come near any man on whom is the mark. Begin at my sanctuary.” Then they began at the old men who were before the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says not to come near anyone with the mark and to “Begin at my sanctuary.” They began with the elders before the house. Arminian readers note that judgment begins with those most responsible, and some hear a hedged echo in 1 Peter 4:17, named without pressing a direct link.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same principle and compare Jeremiah 25:29, “I begin to work evil at the city which is called by my name”, named without harmonizing. They read the verse soberly, observing that those who led in idolatry face judgment first, while the marked are spared.

verses.text: He said to them, “Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go out!” They went out, and struck in the city.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go out!” Arminian readers note the shocking reversal in which the LORD himself orders the defilement of his own house, and they read it soberly as showing that the temple offers no protection to a people in rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reversal and observe that the house is already defiled by idolatry, so the judgment makes its condition visible. They read the verse with sobriety and see in it the warning that sacred places cannot shield those who have abandoned God.

verses.text: While they were killing, and I was left, I fell on my face, and cried, and said, “Ah Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the residue of Israel in your pouring out of your wrath on Jerusalem?”
verses.arminianNotes: While they were killing, Ezekiel fell on his face and cried, “Ah Lord GOD!”, asking whether the LORD would destroy all the residue of Israel. Arminian readers note the prophet’s intercession, and they compare Amos 7:2 and Genesis 18:23–25, named without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same intercession and its echo in 11:13, where Ezekiel asks, “Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?” They read the prophet’s cry as faithful grief for his people, and both traditions see in it a model of prayer in the face of judgment.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great, and the land is full of blood, and the city full of perversion; for they say, ‘The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD doesn’t see.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers that the iniquity of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great, the land full of blood, the city full of perversion, for they say, “The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD doesn’t see”. Arminian readers note the echo of 8:12 and the people’s own excuse turned against them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the LORD’s answer as explaining why the judgment is just. They observe that the people’s saying reverses the order of 8:12, and both traditions read the verse as linking violence, injustice, and unbelief in God’s attention.

verses.text: As for me also, my eye won’t spare, neither will I have pity, but I will bring their way on their head.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “As for me also, my eye won’t spare, neither will I have pity, but I will bring their way on their head.” Arminian readers note that the judgment is described as their own way returning on them, and they see it as the consequence of choices persistently made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same phrase and read it as God’s just recompense for sin. They observe that the LORD’s refusal to pity at this point answers the prophet’s plea without denying that mercy has already been shown through the mark on those who sigh and cry.

verses.text: Behold, the man clothed in linen, who had the inkhorn by his side, reported the matter, saying, “I have done as you have commanded me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The man clothed in linen reported, “I have done as you have commanded me.” Arminian readers note that the report emphasizes the marking of the faithful, and they see the completion of the task as assurance that those who grieved over sin were not forgotten in the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same report and read it as showing that God’s purpose of mercy toward the marked is carried out fully. They observe that the man in linen reappears in chapter 10, and both traditions read his faithful completion of the task as shared ground.
